title: Dream-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds
data_curation: Not a focus of this paper. No model is trained. The only 'data' is the accumulated discovery history: each online round logs a discovery tree in which every node is one generation-evaluation attempt, storing its full generation history, a filesystem snapshot and a fixed-protocol score (root score 0). These trees are appended to a growing pool H_t and reused as replay simulators. The task evaluators provide the ground-truth signal: KernelBench correctness checks against PyTorch with inverse-runtime scoring on an L40S; the Lasso objective check F_k(w) <= F_k(w_sklearn)+1e-6 on fresh instances, with a geometric-mean-runtime score over 17 SimpleTES synthetic instances; and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks x 2 runs) for harnesses.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. Instead of a training curriculum, Dream-RSI alternates online exploration and offline 'dreaming' over T rounds: Lasso 5 rounds (W=10, budget 110 = 10 branches x 11 attempts with Gemini-3.1-Pro; W=32, 640 = 32x20 with Gemini-3.7-Flash), KernelBench 9 rounds, math tasks 10 rounds (110 calls per round), and harness optimization 9 rounds (W=4, 16 = 4x4). Each offline phase evaluates M=4 policy versions (the current policy plus three rewrites), and the replay pool grows every round. An ablation on ConvDiv shows that replaying over the full history beats replaying only the current round (1.90 vs 1.59).
method: Exploration is made programmable through a lightweight orchestration layer: an executable policy picks a batch C of up to W eligible nodes (root or leaves) to expand, which controls branching, parallelism and stopping while the base agent, models and evaluator stay fixed. Each completed tree becomes a deterministic replay world: candidate policies traverse recorded parent-child chains (expanding the root reveals its earliest unrevealed child), so scoring a policy only reads stored outcomes. The replay objective is the normalized hypervolume of the quality-cost Pareto frontier, swept over budget preferences rho in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, minus lambda times a parallelism penalty (sequential rounds per call). A policy-development agent reads replay traces and scores, rewrites the policy code (including a plan_grid width/depth planner and a beta schedule), and the best of the M versions by mean replay score over all worlds is redeployed online. Including the current policy among the candidates guarantees the selected policy is never worse on replay score.
eval_metrics: Nine tasks in four domains, with cost measured as cumulative discovery-agent calls. KernelBench (VGG16, LayerNorm, ConvDiv, ConvMax): performance as 1/ms versus number of generations, against Recursive Fixed Exploration and PACEvolve (48h cap). Math: Sum-Difference (higher is better), Autocorrelation inequality (lower is better), Circle Packing (higher is better), against AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, ThetaEvolve, EvoX and SimpleTES. Lasso path: average runtime (ms) on six held-out datasets (Gisette, RCV1, DNA, Leukemia, Colon, Duke Breast) against sklearn, glmnet and SimpleTES. Harness optimization: Terminal-Bench 2.1 full-suite score against Claude Code (0.75), Terminus-Kira (seed) and Meta-Harness (0.79). Headline numbers: Sum-Diff 1.145427, Circle Packing 2.635983 (ties best), Autocorrelation 1.456375, TB2.1 0.7247->0.8090.
key_results: On KernelBench, Dream-RSI matches fixed exploration with 2.43x (VGG16) and 1.79x (LayerNorm) fewer generations, and reaches 2.09x (ConvDiv) and 1.44x (ConvMax) higher performance at similar budgets. On Lasso it cuts held-out average runtime from 3587.1 to 2931.0 ms with 317 vs 550 calls (Gemini-3.1-Pro), beating sklearn and glmnet on all six datasets with about 162x fewer calls than SimpleTES's 51,200 (different backbones). It also lifts a Terminus-Kira harness on Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 0.7247 to 0.8090, above Meta-Harness (0.79).
evolution_note: Dream-RSI sits in the AlphaEvolve/OpenEvolve/ShinkaEvolve/PACEvolve line of LLM-driven discovery and follows EvoX in treating the search strategy itself as the object to optimize. Drawing on model-based RL and Dreamer-style world models, it addresses the delayed, expensive meta-level feedback of that setting by turning past discovery trees into free off-policy simulators. This closes a recursive self-improvement loop at the exploration-policy layer without any weight updates. Its recorded discovery trees could also serve as training data for the policy-learning RSI approaches in this corpus.
